result: The authors developed a theory showing that dendritic nonlinearities are critical for efficient spike-based computation, with the optimal nonlinearity depending on presynaptic activity statistics. This theory accurately predicted responses of cortical pyramidal cells to glutamate uncaging based on in vivo presynaptic statistics, and NMDA receptor activation was necessary for optimal integration.
evaluation: Claims C2-C4 establish the main theoretical framework and experimental validation. The theory (C3, C21) is mathematically derived and tested experimentally (C4, C41-C48) with appropriate statistical analysis showing significant differences between correct and incorrect presynaptic statistics. The role of NMDA receptors (C23, C51-C52) is demonstrated through pharmacological blockade experiments.

result: The optimal response is linear when presynaptic neurons are independent but becomes nonlinear when they are correlated. Sublinear integration is optimal for second-order correlations (Gaussian random walks), while supralinear integration is optimal for state-switching dynamics with higher-order correlations.
evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by theoretical analysis (Equations 11-14) and computational simulations shown in Figures 1C-D and 2A-F. The distinction between second-order and higher-order correlations determining integration type is mathematically derived and illustrated. C30 extends this to firing rate-based computations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

result: A canonical biophysically-motivated dendritic model with sigmoidal nonlinearity can approximate the optimal response. The same sigmoidal nonlinearity can implement both supralinear and sublinear integration depending on input regime, allowing adaptation to changing presynaptic statistics without parameter changes.
evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are mathematically proven in limiting cases (Materials and methods, Equations 24-29) and demonstrated in Figure 3A-B. C35-C36 show the flexibility of the same nonlinearity across input regimes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), supported by citation to experimental work (C37, Gasparini and Magee 2006).

result: Nonlinear dendrites with clustered connectivity of correlated inputs are necessary to achieve near-optimal estimation performance. Models with linear dendrites or random connectivity performed significantly worse than the clustered nonlinear model.
evaluation: Claims C38 and C40 are supported by computational modeling (Figure 4) with cross-validation and statistical comparisons (n=20 runs, p<10^-13 for all comparisons). The necessity of both clustering and nonlinearity is demonstrated across different parameter regimes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

result: Dendritic integration in neocortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons matches predictions from the optimal response tuned to their respective in vivo presynaptic statistics. Using incorrect presynaptic statistics (second-order correlations only, independence, or wrong brain region) resulted in significantly worse fits.
evaluation: Claims C41-C48 present experimental validation with appropriate sample sizes (n=6 per region), statistical tests (t-tests with reported p-values), and controls. The precision of predictions matched inherent variability (C41-C42: p>0.12) while incorrect statistics gave significantly worse fits (C43-C46: p<0.01). Region-specific tuning (C47-C48, C50) shows interaction between input source and postsynaptic location.

result: NMDA receptor blockade by AP5 resulted in dendritic responses that were poorly fit by the model even after refitting postsynaptic parameters, indicating that fine tuning of dendritic nonlinearities to input statistics relies on NMDA receptor action.
evaluation: Claims C51-C52 are supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5E,J (AP5 condition). The substantially poorer fits after NMDA blockade, even with parameter refitting, provide strong evidence for the necessity of NMDA receptors in implementing the predicted nonlinearities.

result: In cerebellar stellate cells, assuming simple second-order correlations made the optimal response match dendritic responses, while hippocampal or neocortical statistics resulted in substantially poorer fits, demonstrating a double dissociation between cell types and input statistics.
evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by analysis of published data (Abrahamsson et al., 2012) shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2. The double dissociation (cortical cells match cortical statistics, cerebellar cells match second-order correlations) strengthens the main hypothesis about statistics-specific tuning.

result: The theory predicts a tight relationship between presynaptic correlation structure and morphological synaptic clustering on dendrites, with correlated inputs targeting nearby locations and independent inputs innervating distinct dendritic subunits. The relevant correlations are marginal correlations based on long-term statistical dependencies during naturalistic inputs.
evaluation: Claims C62-C63, C65-C66, and C77 state predictions of the theory that await experimental confirmation. While the predictions are logically derived from the theory and supported by some existing literature (C64, C70-C75, C78-C79), direct experimental tests of the predicted correlation-clustering relationship are not provided in this manuscript.

result: The optimal response is computationally complex and unlikely to be directly implemented by neurons. Simple second-order correlations imply sublinear integration via passive dendrites, while supralinear integration for state-switching dynamics likely involves NMDA receptors with graded, tunable plateau potentials.
evaluation: Claims C56-C57 are logical inferences from the computational complexity (storing N^2 variables). C58 is supported by citations to prior work on NMDA-mediated nonlinearities (C59-C60) and the experimental AP5 results (C51-C52). C61 synthesizes these observations with the optimal response properties (Figure 4).

result: Background on dendritic integration: Cortical neurons integrate thousands of synaptic inputs nonlinearly, with dendrites performing sublinear to superlinear integration and various arithmetic operations. While biophysical mechanisms are understood, their role in circuit-level computations is unknown, and existing theories focus on simplified input regimes.
evaluation: Claims C1, C5-C13 establish the background knowledge about dendritic integration, all supported by appropriate citations to prior work. Claims C14-C16 identify gaps in current understanding that motivate the present study. C31-C32 provide mechanistic background also supported by citations.

result: The theoretical approach is based on adaptation to natural input statistics (successful in sensory systems) and recognizes that spike-based communication creates an information bottleneck for analog computations in cortical circuits.
evaluation: Claims C17-C20 establish the conceptual foundation of the theory, supported by citations to relevant prior work. The information bottleneck concept (C20) is well-established in the literature (Pfister et al., 2010; Sengupta et al., 2014).

result: Coordinated state switches in presynaptic populations lead to higher-order statistical dependencies observed in vivo, and prior work showed that hippocampal dendritic integration switches between supralinear (synchronized inputs) and linear (asynchronous inputs) depending on input synchrony.
evaluation: Claim C28 is supported by multiple citations to in vivo studies. Claim C37 cites specific experimental work (Gasparini and Magee, 2006) demonstrating state-dependent integration that aligns with the theory's predictions.

result: Background on synaptic clustering and correlations: Marginal correlations include signal and noise correlations and can be substantial even with small noise correlations. Evidence for synaptic clustering exists in multiple systems, though some studies found interspersion of differently tuned inputs. The relevant statistical dependencies are those during spontaneous activity.
evaluation: Claims C67-C75 and C78-C83 provide background on correlations and clustering, all supported by appropriate citations. C76 presents contradictory evidence, which the authors address by noting differences in experimental paradigms (naturalistic vs. single-dimension stimuli, C77).
